replying_to: Replying to Refining Multimodal Representations using a modality-centric self-supervised module
display_title: Official Review of Paper4381 by Reviewer RxU1

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a novel fusion module namely REFINER for multi-modal information fusion. Specifically, the method can be divided into two steps: (1) A self-supervision learning-based method is proposed for multi-modal representations learning. (2) The fused embedding is applied in the downstream task. In addition, when combined with metric learning, the proposed method can further separate the clusters across modalities and further boost performance.
content.main_review:
Strengths :
(1) The proposed fusion module REFINER could integrate multiple modalities such as vision, text, and image into a uniform expression for downstream tasks learning. 
(2) After being coupled with metric learning, the REFINER module can be leveraged on unlabeled data.
(3) Compared with some baseline models, the proposed method can get better performance gains.
Weaknesses:
In this manuscript, the weaknesses are mainly embodied in the following aspects: 
(1) Innovation, that I am optimistic about the proposed integration module, but I think the novelty of this manuscript is not always sufficient.
(2) Experiments, that some recent work seems to be missed. For example, on the Hateful Memes dataset, I find that NIPS2020[1] has reached a relatively high SOTA, while the results of this article are relatively low compared to it.
[1] Kiela, D., Firooz, H., Mohan, A., Goswami, V., Singh, A., Ringshia, P., & Testuggine, D. (2020). The hateful memes challenge: Detecting hate speech in multimodal memes. arXiv preprint arXiv:2005.04790.
content.summary_of_the_review: First of all, I think the novelty of this manuscript is not always sufficient. Secondly, the experimental results are quite different compared to some other SOTAs, which somewhat makes it hard for readers to convince the effectiveness of this method.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

display_title: Clarification on novelty and the SOTA manuscript reference

content.title: Clarification on novelty and the SOTA manuscript reference
content.comment:
Thank you for these detailed comments.

From the reviewer’s summary, we surmise that the main concern is on the sufficiency of novelty. The main novelty of the paper are -
1. the development of an add-on REFINER module that is designed to reconstruct upstream signals and strengthen their representation in the fused embedding space, 
2. a pooler module that identifies upstream signals for the REFINER module to target, 
3. combining metric learning and refining to improve performance of Multimodal Fusion Modules on Multimodal tasks and 
4. demonstration of inferior unimodal encoding based retrieval of multimodal embeddings, and how RefNet can boost performance by over 10% on top-1 retrieval (results described in the overall response above). We hope the reviewer reconsiders their rating based on the above, along with the performance boost on the datasets and additional studies we have done, that the approach is significantly novel.

"Experiments, that some recent work seems to be missed. For example, on the Hateful Memes dataset, I find that NIPS2020[1] has reached a relatively high SOTA ..." 

We confirmed with the authors of the cited paper above that these numbers are not for the original Hateful Memes dataset. The numbers reported in the cited manuscript during NIPS2020 was only an **AUROC of 70.45** for Vilbert and **67.76** for MMBT (https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.04790v2), and we were able to reproduce those baselines, and demonstrated improvement over the baselines.
The SOTA numbers the reviewer has summarized above are from an updated version of the same arxiv paper a few months before our submission, where all the baseline numbers are reported higher. **We emailed the authors, and they said this was an updated Hateful Memes dataset** (even the reported human reviewer reproducibility is larger than the NIPS2020 version).

Some references backing the baseline numbers we reported in the manuscript on the original Hateful Memes dataset are given below
1. Papers With Code: https://paperswithcode.com/paper/hateful-memes-detection-via-complementary/review/
2. Zhang et al. Hateful Memes Detection Via Complementary Visual and Linguistic Networks (https://arxiv.org/pdf/2012.04977.pdf)
3. Zhou et al. Multimodal Learning for Hateful Memes Detection (http://128.84.4.18/pdf/2011.12870)
4. Sandulescu, Vlad. Detecting Hateful Memes Using a Multimodal Deep Ensemble (https://arxiv-download.xixiaoyao.cn/pdf/2012.13235.pdf)

display_title: Official Review of Paper4381 by Reviewer sr5x

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper presents a self-supervised module that refines representations after multi-modal fusion. The module called REFINER aims to reproduce the pre-fusion representations of each modality from post-fusion embedding. This ensures that the information about each modality is encoded in the fused embedding. The authors experiment with the addition of this module on top of existing fusion methods, such as VILBERT and MMBT, as well as concat, linear sum, etc. The experiments show improvement over baselines under most conditions.
content.main_review:
The additional objectives are simple, and it is practical in that it can be applied to many fusion methods. The method shows improvements over baselines. The choice of dataset for the experiments is reasonable.

However, it is not clear where the improvements come from. It could be that each modality embedding is captured well in the fused embedding, but it could also be just some regularisation effect. It would be helpful to evaluate on uni-modal downsteam tasks.
There is no consistent improvement from metric learning, which is claimed as a key contribution.

The structure of the paper is fine, but there are lots of errors in writing (e.g. networks does not, N-Vidia Volt100, image and test – text I guess?).
content.summary_of_the_review: The addition of per-modality reconstruction module contributes positively to performance. However, more analysis can be done to demonstrate the meaning of the gains.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper4381 by Reviewer sr5x
display_title: Understanding the source of improvements of ReFNet

content.title: Understanding the source of improvements of ReFNet
content.comment:
Thank you for your comments. We are glad that the reviewer felt positively about the performance of our method. We performed additional analysis to understand and demonstrate where the improvements came from. 

We performed the following additional studies:

1. **Unimodal retrieval**: We undertook a study where we performed retrieval using either unimodal image or text encoders as query and the pair of fused embedding and label as (key, value) pair. The model was created using MMBT architecture on the mmIMDB training dataset, and the retrieval was performed using kNN on the mmIMDB test dataset. There was a significant boost by ReFNet over baseline for retrieval using both the image and the text encoder features. For the image encoder features, top-1 retrieval had a boost of over 15%, and top-2 retrieval had a boost of 4+%. The results are described in the table below.

**Retrieval using image encoder features**

|   model | Top-1  | Top-2  | Top-5  |  Top-10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|baseline | 27.44 | 42.83 | 60.51 | 67.02   |  
|ReFNet | 42.67 | 46.99 | 58.15 | 70.05 |
|   |   |   |   |   |

For the text encoders, ReFNet boosted the retrieval by on average 2.7%. The results are provided in the table below, and additional details are in Appendix A.8 of the revised manuscript.

**Retrieval using text encoder features**

|   model | Top-1  | Top-2  | Top-5  |  Top-10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|baseline | 23.30 | 34.26 | 49.45 | 59.26  |  
|ReFNet | 23.66 | 36.40 | 53.05 | 63.82 |
|   |   |   |   |   |

2. **Unimodal task with Multimodal Architecture**: We have added a study wherein we feed in (image, text) pairs where either image or text is not relevant to the downstream task. We then performed baseline runs with only relevant unimodal inputs, and compared with the refiner outputs. Using the text only features, REFINER was able to boost the micro F1 score from 65.9 to **66.9** (**+1%**) and macro F1 score from 56.6 to **57.7** (**+1.1%**) respectively. Using the image only features, REFINER was able to boost the micro-F1 score over MMBT baseline from **47.6** to **48.6**. 
The results show that the refinement does result in better performance. We surmise that this is because multimodal fusion modules do not innately preserve information upstream of the fusion module during training because the high dimensional fusion embeddings driving low dimensional downstream tasks tend to get stuck in local minima, and unless a regularization method such as REFINER is explicitly imposed, that information might be lost. Another interpretation of the refiner is that the architecture tends to find representations closest to the target (which could be unimodal) embeddings that also minimize a downstream cost function.
3. **Ablation on Modality Pooler for REFINER targets**: Choosing a target that is very upstream, such as the raw image pixels or text tokens, can result in the REFINER undoing the cross-modal attention weighting which is the hallmark of Multi-modal transformers. However, choosing a target which is just upstream of the fusion module might not be very relevant as that information might already be represented in the fused embedding. To elucidate how the choice of REFINER target affects outcomes, we performed a study measuring the impact of five different modality pooler operations on the performance. 
The results, summarized below, show that including the penultimate layer on the modality pooling operation improves performance of REFINER compared to just including the last layer, which might indicate that different encoder layers contains relevant modality-specific information  which are not implicitly represented in the fused embeddings. 

|target | macro f1 val. | micro f1 val. | macro f1 test | micro f1 test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|average last layer | 58.85 | 67.21 | 57.64 | 66.76 |
|average last two layers | 59.18 | 67.96 | 58.30 | 67.20 |
| average sum last layer | 58.64 | 68.07 | 58.33 | 67.20 |
| average sum last two layers | 59.05 | 68.09 | 58.66 | 67.78 |
| average concat | 57.55 | 67.22 | 57.75 | 67.48 |

Question: "However, it is not clear where the improvements come from...."

Response: Overall, the ReFNet will help in regularization of the fusion module, and other parts of the architecture that are downstream of the target (REFINER pooler). To tease out the effects of where the improvements came from, we re-analyzed our data and performed additional ablation studies as described above.
In summary, we believe the ReFNetMS showed consistent improvement over REFINER in few shot settings. From the new ablation studies, REFINER boosted performance over baselines for problems with just unimodal inputs or on unimodal retrieval tasks.

We will also update the manuscript to correct errors/omissions and also fix the above issues that the reviewer has pointed out.

replying_to: Replying to Refining Multimodal Representations using a modality-centric self-supervised module
display_title: Official Review of Paper4381 by Reviewer NjUK

content.summary_of_the_paper: The submission proposes a "REFINER" module which can be plugged into an existing multimodal pretraining frameworks, such as VilBERT, as an additional loss. The loss aims at reconstructing unimodal features (e.g. inputs to VilBERT) from the multimodal outputs of a pretraining framework, using MSE, or contrastive loss, etc. The motivation for this is to "ensure ... unimodal and fused representations are strongly encoded in the latent fusion space". The authors demonstrated the effectiveness of their proposed auxiliary training objective by adding it to VilBERT and MMBT. Experiments on "Hateful Memes" and "Multimodal IMDB" benchmarks show improvement over the baselines without "REFINER", especially in the lower-shot setup.
content.main_review:
+ The observation that the encoded "fusion embedding" by VilBERT could lose "unimodal" information is interesting.
+ The proposed solution is simple and can be applied to any existing multimodal pretraining frameworks. Good performance on the included benchmarks.
- I'm confused about the novelty claimed by the authors. Specifically, isn't the feature reconstruction loss exactly what has been implemented by VilBERT (Figure 3a in the original paper)? Although the original VilBERT only used MSE to "reconstruct" the encoded image and text features, there are other work (e.g. [a]) used contrastive learning objectives. My confusion also arises from Figure 6 in the supplementary of the submission, where it seems a single "fused embedding" is returned by the "fusion module", whereas most of the pretraining frameworks, due to the use of transformers, return sequential outputs. Could the authors clarify which output from VilBERT did they choose as the "fused embedding"? According to my current understanding of the proposed method, it appears to me that either the authors used a subset of the possible outputs from the baselines (so that the baselines performed worse), or their proposed method has already been implemented by the baselines.
- On a high-level, why is it desirable to ensure "unimodal and fused representations are strongly encoded in the latent fusion space", give the goal of the additional transformer encoder is to combine the information? If a unimodal reconstruction loss is necessary to ensure unimodal information is not lost, why not directly augment the output of VilBERT with its unimodal inputs? This would make an essential baseline to the proposed method.
- Closely related to the above point, how task-dependent are the current observations? It is especially important considering the authors introduced the OCR modality as input, and avoided the standard benchmarks that VilBERT and numerous vision-language pretraining frameworks have been using.
- Although some are described in the supplementary, more details on the baseline approach would be beneficial to reproduce the results, and understand the contribution clearly.
- I would avoid describing the loss as "self-supervised" given the unimodal representations as inputs are supervised pretrained. It would also be extremely helpful to clarify what "responsibility" refers to.

[a] Learning Video Representations using Contrastive Bidirectional Transformer.
content.summary_of_the_review:
The paper proposed an auxiliary loss for existing multimodal pretraining frameworks, and made interesting observations on how existing approaches might lose "unimodal" information. However, the reviewer has serious concerns on the claimed technical novelty when compared with the baselines, the lack of important ablation studies, and the selection of benchmarks to use. Some concerns are due to the lack of implementation and experimental details from the main submission. Hence at the current stage I recommend rejection of the submission.

**Post rebuttal**

I really appreciate the authors' effort to provide additional results and a detailed rebuttal. The new unimodal results are strong and relevant. However I still do not fully follow the authors' explanation (e.g. unfortunately I do not fully understand from the rebuttal why "optimal fused representation ... should be grounded on information from upstream of the combined representation" was not realized by earlier VL frameworks; I also had a hard time connecting "... imposing some invariance in its representation" with the proposed method). Finally, I still believe that results on the standard benchmarks used by many existing VL pretrained models (e.g. VQA) should be included even if the proposed method does not lead to a gain, that would help the readers understand when the proposed method would be useful.
Due to the reasons above, I cannot recommend acceptance at the moment.

content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

replying_to: Replying to Clarification on novelty and additional studies

content.title: continued
content.comment:
Below, we give a point-by-point response to the other concerns

Q: "I'm confused about the novelty claimed by the authors. .. their proposed method has already been implemented by the baselines.’"

A: In the ViLBERT architecture, though the vision and text channels get their respective embeddings (which use cross-modal key-value pairs to perform fusion), there is a step to combine them together (e.g. element-wise product or sum) to then create a combined representation which is subsequently used for the downstream task. The goal of our manuscript is to get the optimal fused representation, which we hypothesized should be grounded on information from upstream of the combined representation (which may not be purely unimodal, as in the case of ViLBERT).  Even with MMBT, the sequential inputs are “pooled” which is then used for the downstream classification task. We introduce the notion of modality pooling as targets for REFINER, though we understand that modality pooling is not purely unimodal due to cross-modal attention weights. Please look at the response to our next question around why this approach subsequently improves performance on the downstream use-case.

For the ViLBERT, we used the MMF framework, which used an elementwise dot product of the pooled text and pooled image (via CLS) tokens as fused embedding. 

Q: on a high-level, why is it desirable to ensure "unimodal and fused representations are strongly encoded in the latent fusion space", give the goal of the additional transformer encoder is to combine the information? If a unimodal reconstruction loss is necessary to ensure unimodal information is not lost, why not directly augment the output of VilBERT with its unimodal inputs? This would make an essential baseline to the proposed method.

A: We amended the statement since it is not entirely accurate. What we strived to demonstrate in this paper was that a fusion module (which takes in either unimodal featurizers or featurizers with cross-modal dependencies such as ViLBERT) can be strengthened by imposing some invariance in its representation. This can be considered either as (i) regularizing the weights of the fusion module and/or (ii) better initialization of fusion module weights with unlabeled multimodal (paired) data. It is entirely possible that say the Kth from last encoder layer had useful information that was lost or unrepresented in the fused embedding which could have been relevant for the downstream module. There is a counter-argument that if that information was necessary, it would be innately preserved, but we argue that due to the high dimensionality of the fused representations and the propensity for trainers using steepest descent to get stuck in local minima that such regularizations do not happen innately. We hope the reviewer finds our additional studies supportive of this point.

By providing a suite of poolers as potential targets (e.g. average pooling across last K layers, average pooling of Kth layer from the last), and the refiner weights as hyperparameters, we are able to boost the generalization of multimodal representations as evidenced by the comparison of baselines to the runs including ReFNet.  Each augmentation need to be paired with a fusion to integrate that particular input. Therefore, we performed additional experiments to demonstrate that the unimodal encodings are not innately preserved in the fused embedding using an unimodal retrieval experiment (please see above for details).

Q: "Closely related to the above point, how task-dependent are the current observations? It is especially important considering the authors introduced the OCR modality as input, .."

A: The OCR in the figure was only representative of the REFINER to have any number of modalities; we did not include any additional feature over what was there in the baselines. Our goal was to demonstrate that ReFNet can be used as an add-on to several multimodal architectures including MMBT, ViLBERT, GMU, Concat, Lincat etc., and we used datasets where several of these methods had been implemented with documented baselines.

Although some are described in the supplementary, more details on the baseline approach would be beneficial to reproduce the results, and understand the contribution clearly.

We used the MMF framework to get the baseline values (https://github.com/facebookresearch/mmf). Our method was integrated into this framework. We are adding more details on the baseline approach and included additional ablations (as explained earlier) in the revised manuscript.

Q: "I would avoid describing the loss as "self-supervised" ..."

A: Self-supervised loss is meant to only indicate that the REFINER loss does not need labels while the ReFNetMS loss does. We will rephrase to make it clear that the self-supervision is only during the Multi-modal training phase. We also decided to remove reference to “responsibility” as it was a bit confusing and not central to the motivations of the manuscript.

replying_to: Replying to Refining Multimodal Representations using a modality-centric self-supervised module
display_title: Official Review of Paper4381 by Reviewer 1vqe

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes a new architecture for multimodal fusion by using a self-supervised module, called Refiner, that refines multimodal representations using a decoding/defusing module applied downstream of the fused embedding. Essentially, Refiner learns a joint embedding space using metric learning that brings multimodal representations of similar points closer together and others far apart.

On several multimodal fusion datasets, their proposed method achieves stronger performance.
content.main_review:
Strengths:
1. The paper is reasonably well-motivated and well-written.
2. Experiments are conducted on a few datasets and results are promising.

Weaknesses:
1. Not really sure what the 'responsibility condition' is formally defined as and the motivations for this are quite vague.
2. I would have expected ablation studies to ablate each part of the model (e.g., refiner module, multi-similarity loss) instead of just changing the percentage of available data.
3. Not sure what figure 4 'degree of unimodality' means and the main takeaway message from figure 4.
4. The model does show better performance but at the expense of more parameters and training time, so it would be good to discuss the trade-offs here.
5. It would be good to benchmark more comprehensively on a multimodal benchmark like this: https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07502
6. I am confused why there needs to be a reconstruction module in the model, it seems like refining/similarity loss can be applied just in a supervised setting without needing to reconstruct the inputs. Some explanations and ablation studies here would be helpful.
7. Quite a few writing and formatting issues, reference format needs to be fixed too.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, the idea is interesting and there are some promising experimental results. However, there remain major issues with the motivation, ablation studies, and quality of the writing + presentation.

We provide a point-by-point response to the reviewer's comments below.

content.title: continued
content.comment:
We have provided a point-by-point response below. We hope that the reviewer reconsiders their rating based on the additional ablation studies and our clarifications below. 

Q: Not really sure what the 'responsibility condition' is formally defined as and the motivations for this are quite vague.

A: Though very different, our work had some parallels with the work of Zhang et al. (FSPool, 2019b) where the authors define a responsibility condition. We posited that the reconstruction loss drives a subset of the weights of the fusion network to be more ‘responsible’ towards specific modalities. On re-reading however, we agree that this doesn’t add to the motivation of the manuscript’s goals and have decided to remove it in the revised manuscript.

Q: I would have expected ablation studies to ablate each part of the model (e.g., refiner module, multi-similarity loss) instead of just changing the percentage of available data.

A: We performed this study as a part of the Hateful Memes and MMIMDB datasets, which are summarized in the discussion section (“The  relative  contribution of self-supervised loss to the improvement in micro F1 score for the mmIMDB dataset was 46-56%, and the rest was due to contrastive loss.  More than 80% of the relative contribution for Hateful Memes dataset was due to the self-supervised REFINER loss”). We have now included and clarified this in the results section, as well as added results from other ablations that we did not report earlier (choice of loss functions, modality poolers for refiner and suppressing specific modalities).
In particular, we included a set of ablation studies with the REFINER module wherein we ablated the REFINER targets. Five different targets using different modality pooling operations relying on different encoder layers were used. The results showed that the inclusion of penultimate layers on modality pooling for REFINER resulted in improved performance as described in the previous response. Additionally, studies with using only the relevant unimodal signals showed better performance for both image and text  refinement as reported in the updated manuscript.
For ReFNetMS we focussed mainly on the ablations on the label dataset size because the rest of the hyperparameters were explored comprehensively in the original dataset. 

Q: Not sure what figure 4 'degree of unimodality' means and the main takeaway message from figure 4.

A: We have updated the caption to "Relative change in accuracy as we increase the weight of the REFINER reconstruction loss, showcasing that refinement helps improve performance over baseline (a zero weight)." to clarify the main takeaway message.

Q: The model does show better performance but at the expense of more parameters and training time, so it would be good to discuss the trade-offs here.

A: There is no increase in the number of parameters during inference. The effect on training time increase is provided in Appendix A.5 (3-5% larger training time if using REFINER alone, and 30-35% using both REFINER and Multi-Similarity loss). Table 3 and 4 provide relative gains with REFINER alone or using ReFNetMS, and combined with the training time changes, we conclude that in general REFINER provides the best gains normalized to training time change. Because the REFINER and Multi-Similarity modules are required only for loss calculation, there is no change in inference time. We have now included this in the discussion section.

Q: It would be good to benchmark more comprehensively on a multimodal benchmark like this: https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.07502

A: Thanks for pointing us to this work. Based on your other comments, and other reviewer's comments, we felt the more appropriate ablations would be to clarify the motivation and perform additional additional studies on the existing dataset, but this could be a good future study.

Q: I am confused why there needs to be a reconstruction module in the model, it seems like refining/similarity loss can be applied just in a supervised setting without needing to reconstruct the inputs. Some explanations and ablation studies here would be helpful.

A: One of the advantages of our method is that the parameters of the fusion module can be seamlessly initialized or regularized with unlabeled data (as evidenced by the improved performance with less available labeled data). We do agree that the REFINER can act like a regularizer during downstream training and need not reconstruct the inputs, and we have clarified this in the revised manuscript. In fact, in several examples the refinement did not reconstruct the inputs but preserved modality-specific pooling operations.

Q: Quite a few writing and formatting issues, reference format needs to be fixed too.
A: We have re-read and fixed the issues in the updated manuscript.

replying_to: Replying to Refining Multimodal Representations using a modality-centric self-supervised module

content.title: Additional experiments supporting our claims
content.comment:
We thank all the reviewers for their detailed comments on our manuscript. We address some of the common concerns here, and then provide detailed point-by-point responses.

One common question reviewers raised was around more evidence for multimodal fusion architectures missing unimodal information, and additional ablations to understand why ReFNet is showing the reported gains.

Towards these, we performed three studies:

1. **Unimodal retrieval**: We undertook a study where we performed retrieval using either unimodal image or text encoders as query and the pair of fused_embedding and label as (key, value) pair. The model was created using MMBT architecture on the mmIMDB training dataset, and the retrieval was performed using kNN on the mmIMDB test dataset. There was a significant boost by ReFNet over baseline for retrieval using both image and text encoder features. For the image encoder features, top-1 retrieval had a boost of over 15%, and top-2 retrieval had a boost of 4+%. The results are described in the table below.

**Retrieval using image encoder features**

|   model | Top-1  | Top-2  | Top-5  |  Top-10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|baseline | 27.44 | 42.83 | 60.51 | 67.02   |  
|ReFNet | 42.67 | 46.99 | 58.15 | 70.05 |
|   |   |   |   |   |

For the text encoders, ReFNet boosted the retrieval by on average 2.7%. The results are provided in the table below, and additional details are in Appendix A.8 of the revised manuscript.

**Retrieval using text encoder features**

|   model | Top-1  | Top-2  | Top-5  |  Top-10 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|baseline | 23.30 | 34.26 | 49.45 | 59.26  |  
|ReFNet | 23.66 | 36.40 | 53.05 | 63.82 |
|   |   |   |   |   |

2. **Unimodal task with Multimodal Architecture**: We have added a study wherein we feed in (image, text) pairs where either image or text is not relevant to the downstream task (e.g. image taken from an irrelevant dataset paired with a text or vise versa). We then performed baseline runs with only relevant unimodal inputs, and compared with the refiner outputs. Using the text only features, REFINER was able to boost the micro F1 score from 65.9 to **66.9** (**+1%**) and macro F1 score from 56.6 to **57.7** (**+1.1%**) respectively. Using the image only features, REFINER was able to boost the micro-F1 score over MMBT baseline from **47.6** to **48.6**. 
The results show that the refinement does result in better performance. We surmise that this is because multimodal fusion modules do not innately preserve information upstream of the fusion module during training because the high dimensional fusion embeddings driving low dimensional downstream tasks tend to get stuck in local minima, and unless a regularization method such as REFINER is explicitly imposed, that information might be lost. Another interpretation of the refiner is that the architecture tends to find representations closest to the target (which could be unimodal) embeddings that also minimize a downstream cost function.
3. **Ablation on Modality Pooler for REFINER targets**: Choosing a target that is very upstream, such as the raw image pixels or text tokens, can result in the REFINER undoing the cross-modal attention weighting which is the hallmark of Multi-modal transformers. However, choosing a target which is just upstream of the fusion module might not be very relevant as that information might already be represented in the fused embedding. To elucidate how the choice of REFINER target affects outcomes, we performed a study measuring the impact of five different modality pooler operations on the performance. 
The results, summarized below, show that including the penultimate layer on the modality pooling operation improves performance of REFINER compared to just including the last layer, which might indicate that different encoder layers contains relevant modality-specific information  which are not implicitly represented in the fused embeddings. 

|target | macro f1 val. | micro f1 val. | macro f1 test | micro f1 test |
|---|---|---|---|---|
|average last layer | 58.85 | 67.21 | 57.64 | 66.76 |
|average last two layers | 59.18 | 67.96 | 58.30 | 67.20 |
| average sum last layer | 58.64 | 68.07 | 58.33 | 67.20 |
| average sum last two layers | 59.05 | 68.09 | 58.66 | 67.78 |
| average concat | 57.55 | 67.22 | 57.75 | 67.48 |
